detail.abstract: The amount of debt held in the form of student loans has increased substantially, rising from roughly $500 billion in 2006 to $1.2 trillion in 2013, and now surpassing the amount of debt held in credit cards (Board of Governors, 2014). The accumulation of student loans might influence enrollment in higher education, career choices, and numerous other social and economic outcomes and decisions (Millett, 2003; Chambers, 1992; Rothstein & Rouse, 2011). Therefore, measuring student loans in national surveys is important because such data will allow researchers and policy analyst to assess the impact of such debt. Over the last decade the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) has expanded its collection of data on student loans to facilitate research on this topic. The PSID is a national longitudinal survey of individuals and families. The study began in 1968 with surveys collecting data on roughly 18,000 individuals living in 5,000 families. These individuals and their descendants were interviewed annually through 1997 and every other year since 1997. These data have been used in over 3,500 scientific and policy publications, and research has demonstrated that the current sample is representative of the US population (McGonagle et al., 2012). The PSID – Transition into Adulthood Study (TAS) was designed to improve available data on the lives of young adults by interviewing young adults in the PSID families. The PSID – TAS survey was conducted for the first time in 2005, with subsequent interviews held every other year since 2005. The survey includes, among other items, questions assessing the amount of student loans held by respondents. In this report we compare estimates of student loan debt reported in the PSID – TAS with the most commonly used data source on student loans: the National Postsecondary Student Aid Survey (NPSAS). The purpose is to demonstrate the usefulness of the PSID – TAS survey as an instrument for researchers interested in student loans.

detail.abstract: AbstractThis study examines how pollution evolves over time when economic agents act strategically and when the environment exhibits nonlinear ecological feedbacks—features common in climate change and water quality management. The results show that economies can become “locked in” to high-pollution states if emissions rise as the environment deteriorates. Avoiding this outcome requires policies that adapt automatically to environmental conditions. A central finding is that state-dependentenvironmental taxes—taxes that increase when pollution is high—are highly effective in preventing environmental lock-in. These taxes strengthen incentives for agents to reduce emissions exactly when the environment is most vulnerable. Progressive tax schemes, such as quadratic or cubic surcharges, are particularly powerful tools for stabilizing ecosystems that face tipping points or threshold effects. The analysis also shows that leadership matters: a major regulator or country can guide others toward cleaner outcomes by anticipating their responses. However, once environmental taxes are well designed and sufficiently responsive, the additional benefit of leadership becomes small. This means that good tax policy can substitute for political or institutional leadership when coordination is difficult. Overall, the findings recommend adaptive, state-responsive policies that automatically tighten as environmental risks increase, ensuring long-term sustainability and avoiding irreversible ecological damage.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a brief description of the Medicare claims data in the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID). PSID was one of the first national panel studies to link to Medicare claims during the 1990s. Linkages recently resumed with support from the National Institute on Aging. As of 2013, linkages to nearly 20 years of Medicare claims have been made for over 2,000 participants. These data are available under restricted data use contract. Comparisons between the PSID’s Medicare eligible sample in 2007 and beneficiaries in the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey (MCBS) show that the two samples are very similar on a number of demographic and health characteristics, but at the oldest ages PSID respondents report less disability than MCBS respondents. In 2005, approximately 60% of eligible respondents gave permission to link Medicare data to their survey responses; over the next three waves of PSID, an additional 15% of 2005-eligible respondents agreed after being re-asked, so that by 2009 the cumulative percentage of the 2005 cohort providing consent reached 74% (75% by 2011). Altogether, permission to link to claims records was obtained from about 61% of all respondents asked in any of the four waves (2005- 2011). The PSID Medicare eligible sample consists of 5,817 sample members who were age 65 or older in any year from 1991 through 2009; under age 65 but reported receiving Medicare in any year 2005 through 2009; or age 65 or older when they died and year of death was between 1991 and 2009. Approximately 38% of eligible cases altogether were sent to the Medicare Research Information Center (MedRIC) for linkage to Medicare data and about 95% of those sent were successfully matched. Comparisons between the eligible sample and the sample successfully linked shows that the proportion of individuals in PSID’s core (“SRC”) sample and who are of white, non-Hispanic race are slightly over-represented among those linked.

detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of severe climate challenges and green energy transition, a critical issue in green governance is whether the new energy demonstration city policy (NEDCP) exacerbates enterprises greenwashing (GWS) and how to effectively mitigate GWS under climate risks. Based on a double machine learning model, this paper investigates the impact of NEDCP on GWS and examines the heterogeneous moderating mechanisms of climate risk perceptions (RPS), including chronic (CRP), severe (SRP) and transitional (TRP) climate risks. The key results are summarized below: First, NEDCP exacerbates GWS. Second, the moderating effect of RPS exhibits notable heterogeneity. Both CRP and SRP exert a negative moderating effect, which weakens the greenwashing effect of the policy, with CRP showing a stronger inhibitory impact. By contrast, TRP exerts a positive moderating effect, which amplifies the role of NEDCP in exacerbating GWS. Third, the heterogeneity reveals that mature, state-owned, and large-scale enterprises are the key groups where NEDCP exacerbates GWS, and the moderating mechanisms also show distinct differences among these enterprises. These conclusions provide empirical evidence for effectively mitigating the GWS exacerbated by new energy policies and optimizing green governance through the effective management of RPS.

title: Dynamic Policy Development and Implementation: An Electoral Accountability Model
affiliations: Princeton University, Department of Politics, Students and

detail.title: Dynamic Policy Development and Implementation: An Electoral Accountability Model
detail.abstract: We study a model in which a politician chooses whether and when to implement a policy during a two-period term before an election. Politicians differ in their ability to develop a policy that will produce outcomes voters value. In each period, the politician privately observes the policy's quality and decides whether to implement it. Once implemented, a well-designed policy may succeed before the election, whereas a badly designed policy never does. Voters observe whether and when policy is implemented, but not its quality, absent visible success. In equilibrium, competent politicians implement policy if and only if it is well-designed. Incompetent politicians implement poorly designed policy-especially late in their term-to mimic a competent politician who either failed to develop a well-designed policy or whose policy has yet to produce results. A central implication is that policies implemented early are, in expectation, of higher quality than those implemented later.

The article deals with three aspects of direct selling business from legal perspective. Firstly, it deals with the major problems that plague the direct selling business, including confusion and overlapping laws while pointing out its benefits. Then the article goes on to emphasize how fraudulent business schemes, which look similar in marketing organization and compensation structure of the direct selling businesses, prevail and tarnish the reputation of genuine direct selling businesses. This is done by indulging in a detailed discussion on the various definitions of direct selling business and related activities that are prohibited by law. The author differentiates among the different concepts to bring clarity to the concept of direct selling business. 

Thereafter, the author ventures into a discussion on the prevailing laws that tend to regulate direct selling and prohibit related concepts and the jurisdictional issues it brings up while explaining the problems that the enforcement agencies. 

The author finally stretches into a deliberation on the ideal regulator for direct selling businesses and why it is need of the hour.

title: Persistent and transient inefficiency in China’s provincial energy demand: A four-component stochastic frontier model

detail.title: Persistent and transient inefficiency in China’s provincial energy demand: A four-component stochastic frontier model

publicationDetails.detailsText: []

detail.abstract: Improving energy efficiency is essential to facilitate the clean energy transition and realize decarbonization targets under the Paris Agreement. This means thataccurately measuring energy efficiency is vitally important. Standard measures of energy efficiency, such as energy intensity and two-step frontier procedures, can confound noise with inefficiency and induce omitted-variable bias. We develop a one-step, four-component stochastic demand frontier that separates unobserved heterogeneity from inefficiency, decomposes inefficiency into persistent and transient parts, and places observed drivers in the log-mean of the transient term. A Bayesian estimator provides joint inference for the frontier, the decomposition, and driver effects. Applying our estimation method to a panel of 30 provinces in China over the period 2003–2021, we find that excluding drivers tends to overstate energy efficiency, while including them lowers the share attributed to persistence—below one-half in several provinces—and elevates the role of short-run factors. Transient efficiency averages about 0.89 versus roughly 0.69 for persistent efficiency. The unified design yields internally consistent, noise-robust efficiency measures and policy-relevant benchmarks that distinguish near-term operational levers from longer-horizon structural reforms.

title: Regulatory Design and Strategic Patenting under the Hatch-Waxman Act

detail.title: Regulatory Design and Strategic Patenting under the Hatch-Waxman Act

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author reports no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract:
The Hatch–Waxman Act created FDA-administered market exclusivities intended to balance innovation incentives with generic competition. While prior work documents effects on prices, entry, and litigation, less is known about how the design of market exclusivity conditions firms’ patent portfolio behavior at the first loss of baseline patent protection. This paper examines how the stock of FDA Orange Book–listed patents evolves around the earliest listed patent expiration (“first patent cliff”), and whether post-expiration dynamics differ systematically across exclusivity regimes.

Using the universe of Orange Book listings from 1985–2019, I construct a drug–year panel and exploit variation in the timing of each drug’s earliest listed patent expiration to estimate event-time difference-in-differences and stacked event-study specifications with drug fixed effects. Patent portfolios contract after the first patent cliff, but the magnitude of contraction varies sharply with regulatory protection. By three years post-expiration, drugs that never receive exclusivity experience substantially greater portfolio contraction relative to the year before expiration, whereas drugs that ever receive exclusivity maintain roughly one additional patent at the same horizon. Among exclusivity recipients, drugs with narrower or conditional exclusivities (pediatric and other add-on categories) exhibit substantially larger post-expiration portfolio declines than drugs with broad, novelty- or rarity-based exclusivities (New Chemical Entity and Orphan Drug exclusivity), with a gap of approximately 1.1 patents by three years post-expiration. Differences across groups are not driven by a discrete inflection in the years immediately preceding expiration.

These results indicate that market exclusivity design—beyond duration—is systematically associated with patent portfolio dynamics following the first patent cliff. Heterogeneity is largest among drugs with more extensive pre-expiration patent portfolios, where firms have greater scope for portfolio adjustment.

detail.abstract: This study empirically examines the causal relationship between the rising cost of housing and household energy stress, utilizing a fixed effects instrumental variable approach and household panel data from Australia over the period 2005 to 2019. Our instrumental variable leverages differences in average housing costs across local government areas (LGAs), driven by differential inflows of foreign investment, reflecting historical spatial variation in the LGAs where immigrants live. Our findings suggest that for a 10 percent increase in the cost of housing, there is a 0.5 percentage-point higher likelihood of experiencing energy poverty. Heterogeneity analysis suggests that renters, homeowners with a mortgage and households with lower educated primary income earners are particularly vulnerable to the adverse effect of the higher cost of housing on energy stress.

title: Is it possible to have legal knowledge without legal inference?
affiliations: Deakin University, Geelong, Australia - Deakin Law School

detail.title: Is it possible to have legal knowledge without legal inference?

declarations.funderStatement: Funded by a Deakin Business and Law Faculty Research Grant Scheme

detail.abstract: Is there a systematic and proper method of legal reasoning or is legal reasoning more open-ended and organic and leading to pluralistic conclusions? I refer to a system of legal inference as  a system of legal reasoning that fits the first description; ie there is a systematic and proper methodology for drawing conclusions based on certain premises. Rules of legal inference tell us how to reason to the correct interpretation of statutes or resolution of cases based on the facts before us. I argue that legal knowledge is not possible without there being at least one system of legal inference leading to a unique legal solution (although what we consider to be a legal solution could be trivalent: true, false or indeterminate). If this kind of legal inference is impossible then law will be arbitrary or permits inconsistency. Thus, those who deny the possibility of legal inference must grapple with serious consequences for the possibility of legal knowledge.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Transforming Micro and Small Enterprises in the Commerce Sector: A Systematic Review

detail.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Transforming Micro and Small Enterprises in the Commerce Sector: A Systematic Review
detail.abstract: The main objective of this article is to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the future of micro and small enterprises (MSEs) in the commerce sector by identifying its principal applications, challenges, and opportunities through a systematic literature review. The study adopts a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) methodology, following the guidelines proposed by Kitchenham and Charters (2007). Academic databases, particularly Scopus, were consulted, and rigorous inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied to select peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2024 that address AI adoption in MSEs within the commercial sector. The findings indicate that AI provides strategic tools that enhance operational efficiency, support informed decision-making, and strengthen competitiveness, especially in areas such as inventory optimization, personalization of customer experiences, and automation of business processes. Nevertheless, the results also highlight persistent barriers faced by MSEs, including limited access to financial resources, shortages of skilled human capital, and the digital divide, all of which constrain the effective adoption of AI technologies. Despite these challenges, AI emerges as a significant opportunity for MSEs to adapt to evolving market dynamics, improve profitability, and reinforce their competitive positioning. The study concludes that AI should be understood not only as a productivity-enhancing tool, but also as a catalyst for innovation and long-term sustainability in an increasingly dynamic economic environment. In this context, the role of governments and institutional actors is essential in promoting supportive policies, targeted financing, and capacitybuilding initiatives that facilitate digital transformation and technological inclusion among MSEs..

detail.title: The Effect of National Minimum Wage Increases on Health in the United Kingdom

detail.abstract: Background: While a growing body of research has examined the effects of the UK National Minimum Wage (NMW) on health, no study has yet evaluated its impact during the COVID-19 pandemic—a period of heightened economic vulnerability. This quasi-experimental study investigates whether annual NMW increases between 2019 and 2023 influenced psychological distress, smoking behaviour, and financial perceptions among low-wage workers. Methods: Using data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study, we applied a difference-in-differences framework to assess the effects of annual NMW adjustments on self-reported mental health, cigarette use, and perceived financial difficulty. The sample comprised hourly paid employees aged 25–64, where the treatment group consisted of workers directly affected by wage increases, and the control group included comparable workers unaffected by NMW. Robustness was assessed through multiple sensitivity analyses. Results: NMW increases were associated with modest improvements in psychological distress (−5.2% in 2019; −9.4% in 2022), strain (−6.8% in 2020), and sleep loss (−6.8% in 2020; −12% in 2023). Improvements were also observed in financial perceptions, with reduced reports of current financial difficulty (−4% in 2019; −7.6% in 2022) and anticipated future difficulty (−9.6% in 2022). No effects were found for smoking. Conclusion: This study provides evidence that recent UK NMW increases yielded modest short-term improvements in mental health and financial well-being among low-wage workers, particularly during the early (2020) and later stages (2022) of the COVID-19 pandemic. These findings support the role of targeted wage policies in mitigating psychological and financial strain during periods of economic disruption.

title: A Measure-Theoretic View of Large Language Models as Stochastic Conditional Operators

detail.title: A Measure-Theoretic View of Large Language Models as Stochastic Conditional Operators
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are often described via architecture and optimization heuristics, while the underlying mathematical object computed at inference time is seldom made explicit. We formalize an LLM as a stochastic conditional operator mapping contexts to probability measures over a token space. Inference becomes conditional expectation with respect to these induced measures; training becomes a variational optimization over conditional distributions under divergence-based objectives. This perspective cleanly separates the conceptual object (a conditional probability kernel) from the parametric implementation (a neural network), clarifies the roles of sampling and decoding, and yields a natural interface with belief updating and decision-making under uncertainty.

title: Losing your Edge When it Counts: Expertise and Evidence Interpretation in High-Stakes Policy Contexts

detail.title: Losing your Edge When it Counts: Expertise and Evidence Interpretation in High-Stakes Policy Contexts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no relevant or material financial interests that relate to the research described in this paper. The findings, interpretations, and conclusions expressed in this paper are entirely those of the authors.

detail.abstract: How well do policy experts interpret statistical evidence when decisions carry high stakes? Received wisdom holds that turning to experts is critical, as their training affords greater technical competence. However, when stakes are high, expert judgement may also be shaped by contextual factors that affect inference. We study this question using a survey experiment conducted at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when decisions about lockdowns were highly salient and contested. We draw on two samples in Germany: development professionals working in international development organizations, and a representative sample of the general public. Participants were tasked with interpreting simple two-by-two frequency tables, which were framed either neutrally (the effect of skin cream on a rash) or in a domain-relevant policy context (the effect of pandemic lockdowns on mortality). We report three main findings: First, development professionals display substantially higher accuracy than the general public, consistent with stronger technical expertise. Second, this expert advantage disappears when identical information is framed within their professional domain: while professionals outperform the general public under the neutral frame, their accuracy falls sharply under the lockdown frame, converging to the performance of lay respondents. Third, contrary to canonical motivated numeracy predictions, this decline is not explained by belief-based mechanisms: prior beliefs about lockdown effectiveness do not differentially predict accuracy among experts. Our findings highlight a boundary condition on the effectiveness of subject-matter expertise in high-stakes policy contexts.

title: Geopolitics of Climate Policy
affiliations: , Manila Observatory and Manila Observatory

detail.title: Geopolitics of Climate Policy
detail.abstract: Climate negotiations and modelling still lack a rigorous way to account for geopolitics. Integrated assessment models, carbon-club scenarios, and pledge trackers typically treat cooperation, promised finance, and supply-chain adaptation as exogenous or implicitly assured. They excel at mapping technically feasible pathways but underspecify the political conditions under which those pathways can be delivered. This blind spot helps explain why observers are repeatedly surprised by shortfalls that were, in principle, predictable from the strategic behaviour of a few pivotal actors. We address this gap with a transparent geopolitics model designed to complement physical and economic models rather than replace them. Our approach combines game theory, public-goods economics, and Monte Carlo simulations. First, we derive evidence-based bargaining profiles for major economies and key financial and technological institutions, based on preferences (domestic incentives and stated NDCs), salience (how climate ranks against growth, jobs, energy, and security), and capacity (legal authority, fiscal space, technology, and administrative capability). Second, we specify the “production function” of climate cooperation across pillars— additive cuts in CO₂, weakest-link logics for methane and leakage, threshold and bestshot logics for standards, grids, and key technologies. Third, we run thousands of simulations that vary elections, shocks, policies, finance, and permitting speed to generate a distribution of politically plausible outcomes rather than a single forecast. From these runs we construct a Geopolitical Feasibility Index (GFI): the share of an IPCC-consistent package that is politically deliverable under current conditions. The index is decomposable by pillar and by actor, allowing users to trace how specific frictions depress outcomes and which coalitions or instruments close the gap most efficiently. In our baseline scenarios, the composite GFI for 2030 clusters at roughly one-third of the ambition required for a 1.5°C-consistent path and declines further by 2035 as temperature limits tighten and grid absorption constraints bind. The framework offers negotiators, finance ministers, climate policy makers and modellers a tractable way to integrate geopolitics into climate scenarios and to prioritise reforms and coalitions where they shift global outcomes most.

title: Clarifying Crypto: A Unified Market Structure Taxonomy
affiliations: William & Mary Law School

detail.title: Clarifying Crypto: A Unified Market Structure Taxonomy
detail.abstract:
This Article confronts a fundamental paradox of today's digital economy: crypto has become a multitrillion-dollar sector increasingly central to federal policy, yet consensus on basic legal and economic questions remains dangerously thin. As Washington considers sweeping market-structure reforms, that disconnect undermines effective oversight, leaving policymakers struggling to distinguish genuine innovation from speculative ambiguity. 

The Article bridges these doctrinal and regulatory gaps through a comprehensive, data-driven taxonomy that organizes the universe of 10,000-plus crypto instruments into distinct categories based on legal and economic reality-substance, not label or form. The framework demonstrates that most legitimate crypto assets closely parallel familiar constructs-such as debt, equity, and loyalty rewards-and should be regulated as such. The analysis also shows how crypto assets lacking discernible rights or coherent analogs often reflect obfuscation rather than novelty. 

Leveraging this multi-faceted framework, the Article proposes a policy blueprint of actionable reforms to rationalize the regulatory architecture, enhance consumer protection, and harmonize jurisdictional frictions at a most critical legislative juncture.

title: Private Equity Fund Formation and Structure: Evidence from the UK

detail.title: Private Equity Fund Formation and Structure: Evidence from the UK
detail.abstract: This paper introduces and summarizes a new data set of limited partnerships and funds of UK-based private equity (PE) investors. I am able to manually extract data from Companies House filings for approximately 1,000 limited partnerships raised by almost 200 general partners (GPs) from 2000 to 2025. This amounts to over 25,000 commitments to PE funds made by around 3,000 different institutional investors located in 70 different countries, and over 3,000 individual investors. I complement this with data from other publicly-available resources to reconstruct the full fund structure of the PE funds in the sample. I first discuss the institutional and regulatory background to PE fund formation, and discuss popular structures used by PE investors when establishing funds. I then provide an overview of the data provided in Companies House filings covering limited partnerships, limited partners (LPs) and capital commitments made into funds. Similar to an increasing trend of PE investors establishing acquisition vehicles used in UK PE buyouts in offshore jurisdictions, the data suggests a sharp rise in the use of offshore-domiciled fund vehicles over the last decade. Together, this reflects an increasing opacity of the UK PE market, at a time when the industry is beginning to advance into the retail investor market.

title: Does Intimate Partner Violence Increase the High Fertility Behavior in Pakistan?
affiliations: , University of Strasbourg, Dubai Islamic Bank Pakistan Limited (DIBPL) and University of Calabria

detail.title: Does Intimate Partner Violence Increase the High Fertility Behavior in Pakistan?
detail.abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a devastating consequence of gender inequality in society. It is the most common type of domestic violence, with intimate partners perpetrating the majority of abuse, leading to negative health outcomes for women. Women who have experienced violence are also at a greater risk of reproductive health effects, inconsistent and lower contraceptive use, and unexpected fertility outcomes. Despite several policies and programs aimed at lowering fertility, Pakistan's fertility rate remains high, indicating a variety of underlying issues. This research investigates whether women's exposure to domestic violence is a contributing factor to increased fertility in Pakistan. We used data from the Pakistan Demographic and Health Survey 2017-2018. A weighted sample of 3,416 currently married women in Pakistan was analyzed. Our dependent variable is the number of children ever born, which serves as a proxy for fertility, and the main explanatory variable is intimate partner violence. An instrumental variable Poisson generalized method of moments estimation was employed to estimate the relationship between IPV and fertility in Pakistan. Our findings support the hypothesis that women who have experienced domestic violence have greater fertility rates compared to those who have not. This result is robust to sensitivity analysis. Our study makes two contributions to the literature. First, it fills a gap in existing research on IPV and fertility in the context of Pakistan. Second, it addresses the endogeneity between IPV and fertility.

title: Beyond the Event Horizon: Post-Event Dynamics in Risk-Adjusted Returns

detail.title: Beyond the Event Horizon: Post-Event Dynamics in Risk-Adjusted Returns
detail.abstract: This paper documents a novel empirical regularity in event-driven asset pricing: risk-adjusted returns peak in the immediate post-event period rather than before events. Analyzing 89,500 earnings announcements and FDA announcements from 2000-2024, I find return-to-variance ratios exhibit dramatic amplification during the five trading days following events compared to pre-event periods. The pattern is robust across firm size quintiles, industries, liquidity levels, and time periods. Using panel regressions with firm and time fixed effects, I show the post-event return advantage persists after controlling for firm characteristics. The findings challenge conventional focus on pre-event positioning and suggest that post-event periods exhibit economically significant deviations from standard risk-return relationships. The results are consistent with several potential mechanisms including time-varying volatility structures, information diffusion dynamics, and behavioral expectation formation.

title: Women's Participation in Various Economic Activities: The Case of Bangladesh

detail.abstract: This research deals the peculiarities and aspects of the participation of Bangladeshi women in various economic activities. The aim of the research to analyze how actively women are involved in the economy and how much time they spend on unpaid housework, depending on age, place of residence and education. It is concluded that regardless of age, place of residence, level of education or marital status, women spend more time on unpaid housework and childcare than men. Given their level of education and place of residence (urban and rural), urban women spend more time in paid work than rural women, while the burden of domestic work is the same for both urban and rural women.

title: Algorithmic Transparency and Portfolio Choices: Field Evidence
affiliations: University of Cergy-Pontoise - THEMA, Laboratoire d'Economie d'Orléans (LEO) and Laboratoire d'Economie d'Orléans, Université d'Orléans

detail.title: Algorithmic Transparency and Portfolio Choices: Field Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether profile-based explanations influence investors' acceptance of algorithmic risk recommendations in a randomized controlled trial embedded directly in the platform's interface of a leading French robo-advisor. Users were assigned either to see graphical explanations of the drivers underlying their recommended risk score and associated portfolio or to receive the standard interface with no explanation. Our results, obtained in a real-world setting with actual clients of a FinTech, do not support the adherence gains from increased transparency that are widely anticipated in the literature. Overall, providing profile-based explanations is not found to increase acceptance of the recommended profile nor raise users' engagement with the platform. However, we find a heterogeneous treatment effect as profilebased explanations lead to a greater downward deviation among desktop users who have already deviated to safer-than-recommended portfolios, but this pattern disappears once users' experience of the platform is taken into account. We observe non-causal evidence in both conditions that behavior is shaped primarily by the digital context and experience: phone and first-time users are more likely to accept the portfolio recommendation than desktop and returning users. While such transparency-enhancing profile-based explanations are informative, they are not a universal lever for adherence, suggesting that explanation design should be tested and tailored across device types and users' experience.

detail.abstract: Debates surrounding universal healthcare have historically focused on coverage models, financing mechanisms, and political feasibility. While these elements are essential, they are insufficient to ensure equitable, safe, and sustainable healthcare delivery. This paper argues that universal healthcare systems fail not primarily due to cost or ideology, but because they are built without adequate attention to administrative accountability, documentation integrity, and system adaptability. Using a systems-based framework, this paper introduces the Universal Care Infrastructure (UCI) model, a modular, auditable, and adaptive approach to universal healthcare design. The model emphasizes administrative harm as a public health risk, positions documentation integrity as a core safety function, and proposes governance mechanisms that allow healthcare systems to evolve without destabilization. By addressing both the visible and invisible determinants of healthcare access and quality, this paper offers a pragmatic pathway toward a universal healthcare system that is scalable, resilient, and centered on human outcomes rather than political abstraction.

title: Women At the Table: Assessing the Effect of Gender Diversity on Firm Performance

detail.title: Women At the Table: Assessing the Effect of Gender Diversity on Firm Performance
detail.abstract: This study aims to assess the relationship between female representation on corporate boards and firm financial performance in the context of Bangladesh's emerging economy. While global research presents mixed findings on board gender diversity effects, empirical evidence from developing countries remains limited, particularly in South Asian contexts where cultural and economic factors may influence governance-performance relationships differently than in developed markets. This study employs panel data collected from published annual reports of 74 companies listed on the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) spanning the period from 2019 to 2022, utilizing both the www.dsebd.org database and individual company websites for data verification. Panel data regression techniques including fixed effect models, random effect models, and Panel Corrected Standard Error (PCSE) models examine gender diversity effects measured through proportion of women directors, binary presence variables, and Blau heterogeneity index on firm performance proxied by return on assets (ROA) and Tobin's Q ratios. The results reveal that female representation on board shows a significant negative relationship with ROA and Tobin's Q, with regression coefficients of-0.02 and-0.40 respectively, indicating deteriorating performance effects as women's board participation increases. Large firms show insignificant relationship between gender diversity and performance metrics, while smaller firms demonstrate significant negative impacts when female family members comprise board positions. The findings of this study suggest that increased female representation in boardrooms may signal negative market perceptions to shareholders in Bangladesh's developing economy context, particularly for smaller firms where family-based appointments are more prevalent.

title: Informativeness and Welfare Effects of Labels: Evidence from the EU Energy Label Re-scaling
affiliations: ETH Zürich - CER-ETH - Center of Economic Research at ETH Zurich, Yale University and University of Otago

detail.title: Informativeness and Welfare Effects of Labels: Evidence from the EU Energy Label Re-scaling
detail.abstract: Information framing can influence economic choices. We investigate the impact of a re-scaling of the EU energy label for appliances on the choices of Swiss consumers. We find that consumers bought more efficient washing machines after re-scaling, with weaker results for fridges and dishwashers. We show that the re-scaling may have improved consumer informativeness as well as welfare for certain types of Swiss washing machine buyers, with weaker results for fridge and dishwasher consumers consumers. Ultimately, the impact of the re-scaling depends on availability of energy-efficient choices, label informativeness as well as consumer preferences for energy efficiency.

detail.abstract: We investigate the impact of monetary policy on the growth and financing expectations of euro area SMEs. Using firm-level data from the ECB's Survey on Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE) from 2009 to 2024, we distinguish between conventional interest rate adjustments and unconventional measures. While conventional tightening consistently dampens expectations regarding turnover and credit, unconventional easing elicits ambiguous responses, consistent with a signalling channel where interventions are interpreted as indicators of future macroeconomic distress. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that firm size, credit history, and borrowing constraints significantly moderate these effects. We find that the interest rate and inflation expectation channels dominate transmission, whereas the bank-lending channel plays a subordinate role. These results suggest that the signalling effects of unconventional policy may dampen its efficacy for constrained firms.

title: Context and Mixed Strategy Equilibrium

detail.title: Context and Mixed Strategy Equilibrium
detail.abstract: The predictive power of mixed-strategy equilibria varies across settings. Laboratory experiments often deviate from equilibrium predictions, while high-stakes professional behaviour frequently conforms. This contrast is usually attributed to expertise, yet professional subjects behave similarly to students in abstract laboratory games. We argue that context, rather than professional status, drives this pattern. In a laboratory experiment based on a simplified Penalty Kick game, we vary contextual framing while holding the game and incentives fixed. Context affects equilibrium play selectively and non-monotonically: video-based context improves conformity for high-imagery ability Strikers, while text-based context increases deviations.

detail.abstract: The deadline for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is fast approaching in 2030, yet progress in many areas remains slower than expected. The knowledge generated by universities plays a central role in meeting these goals within the established timeframe. In this context, analyzing how universities perform in producing relevant knowledge for the SDGs becomes critically important. However, there is still limited empirical evidence on how universities are contributing to this agenda, particularly in middle-income countries such as Mexico. This study examines publication and specialization patterns in SDG-related scientific output across 15 of Mexico's most productive universities from 2015 to 2023. Using SciVal (based on Scopus), a set of bibliometric indicators was developed to assess dimensions such as impact, citation, collaboration type, and relative specialization. The findings indicate that publications related to the SDGs have increased at a faster rate than total scientific output across all institutions. These universities specialize in a diverse range of SDGs, with particular emphasis on SDGs 2 (Zero Hunger), 14 (Life Below Water), and 15 (Life on Land). Additionally, new cases of specialization and extraordinary growth were documented in a group of SDGs referred to as "social" due to their alignment with social science disciplines (e.g., SDGs 1, 4, 5, 8, 10, and 16). These results provide valuable evidence for science policy and highlight the importance of strengthening the role of universities as key actors in addressing global and local sustainability challenges.

detail.abstract: The rapid aging of populations has prompted the introduction of social pension programs aimed at preserving the welfare of the elderly. However, adverse socioeconomic behaviors may dampen the intended policy effects. Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, this study examines the impact of social pension receipt on expenditure patterns and material hardship among older adults aged 80 year or older in Vietnam. We find that social pension increases the risk of material hardship in rural areas and reduces non-food expenditures in urban areas. To explain these findings, we explore two potential pathways: economic behavioral mechanisms and social behavioral mechanisms. The results suggest that behavioral responses may offset the intended welfare benefits of social pensions, underscoring the need to account for such adjustments in the design of aging-related policies in developing countries.

detail.abstract: The objective of the study is to examine the effect of abnormal credit supply on selected macroeconomic performance indicators in ECOWAS countries. In the study, abnormal credit supply refers to the abnormal (or sudden, unexpected) decrease or increase in the level of credit supply in the economy at a particular period in ECOWAS countries. The study used data for ECOWAS countries obtained from World Bank database during the 1993 to 2021 period. The model specification expresses macroeconomic performance as a function of abnormal credit supply and controlling for the effect of banking sector characteristics, institutional factors, and central bank size on macroeconomic performance. The empirical results showed that large abnormal cuts in credit supply decreases GDP growth in ECOWAS countries. The empirical results also show that large abnormal cuts in credit supply leads to a significant fall in the standard of living (or GDP per capita) in ECOWAS countries. The empirical results also show that abnormal increase in credit supply lowers the rate of inflation in ECOWAS countries. Finally, a uni-directional relationship between abnormal increase in credit supply and the rate of inflation was found. The primary contribution to knowledge of this study is its extension of our understanding of the role of credit supply for better macroeconomic outcomes. The study provides new knowledge by focusing on the impact of abnormal credit supply on selected indicators of macroeconomic performance in the context of ECOWAS countries - a context that has not been examined in the economic literature. The findings are useful to monetary policy decision makers in their evaluation of the optimal amount of credit supply that is needed to support economic growth in ECOWAS countries. The policy implication of this result is that large abnormal cuts in credit supply is undesirable because it hinders economic growth and has an undesirable welfare effect on the standard of living in ECOWAS countries, thereby worsening economic output per person. The recommendation of the study is that policy makers in ECOWAS countries should be cautious when introducing economic policies – whether fiscal policy, monetary policy or regulatory policy – so as not to introduce economic policies that will trigger financial institutions to unexpectedly decrease credit supply which can ultimately hinder growth and macroeconomic performance.

detail.abstract: This paper conceptualizes iDemocracy, a digital-age democratic model that reconstructs civic sovereignty through continuous participation, dynamic authorization, and market-based coordination. Departing from both representative and online voting systems, iDemocracy embeds democratic decision-making in a policy-exchange environment where preferences are continuously aggregated and revised. Through mechanisms of policy exchange institutionalization, political fund organization, and revocable authorization, the model transforms democracy from periodic delegation to ongoing collective deliberation. The study further introduces the iDemocracy Party-an institutional party form that operationalizes procedural neutrality within existing representative frameworks. Together, these mechanisms demonstrate how democratic legitimacy may shift from "who represents" to "how representation is procedurally realized," offering a systemic pathway for aligning democratic institutions with the information structures of the digital age and structurally mitigating ideological polarization and political corruption.

This novel category addresses failures where organizations-despite possessing capital adequacy and operational integrity-collapse due to "phase lag" and "dyschrony" relative to environmental dynamics. detail.abstract: This research investigates the predictive efficacy of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for directional equity forecasting within the Indian banking sector. Utilizing historical daily returns from five systemically important banks (HDFC, ICICI, SBI, Axis, and Kotak) between 2020 and 2024, the study demonstrates that market noise can be effectively filtered to reveal structural alpha. The methodology utilizes PCA to extract orthogonal components, followed by a Random Forest classification architecture. A critical discovery of this research is that PC3 despite explaining only 7.71% of total variance holds the highest predictive feature importance (0.3460), suggesting that directional signals are often embedded in idiosyncratic sector spreads rather than broad market variance. The resulting model achieves a 55.06% accuracy and a 77.34% recall for upward price movement. detail.abstract: Switzerland's net-zero transition substantially reduces climate impacts but also risks shifting health burdens abroad, as our analysis shows. We provide the first comprehensive, semi-regionalized assessment for Switzerland that quantifies and monetizes health damages, expressed as disabilityadjusted life years (DALYs), from both climate change and particulate matter (PM 2.5) formation across the full life cycle. Our novel approach, using new region-specific characterization factors and a 56-region damage account, shows that the 2050 net-zero pathway cuts total health impacts by 54% compared to 2020. However, this progress comes with a hidden cost: over 80% of the remaining burden occurs outside Switzerland, primarily from PM 2.5 formation in European and Asian supply chains. Expressed in externalcost intensities, electrified transport shows low social costs, while small-scale biomass combustion remains a high-cost, predominantly domestic option. Our study offers policymakers clear metrics to pair rapid decarbonization with cleaner upstream supply chains and targeted pollution controls.

title: Stages of Implementation and Multi-Actor Contributions in Community-Based Adaptation: A Semi-Systematic Review of Academic Case Studies

detail.title: Stages of Implementation and Multi-Actor Contributions in Community-Based Adaptation: A Semi-Systematic Review of Academic Case Studies
detail.abstract: Adapting to climate change in ways that are both effective and socially just is a challenge that requires collaborative efforts and locally grounded responses. Climate change increasingly threatens communities that have contributed least to its causes, while the involvement of these communities is crucial for designing adaptation measures that are context-specific, inclusive, and sustainable. Community-based adaptation (CBA) addresses this challenge by emphasising bottom-up adaptation processes. As CBA has gained prominence in both research and practice, an expanding body of case studies has documented its application across diverse contexts. However, conceptual frameworks of the CBA implementation process still lack systematic grounding in case study evidence. To address this gap, our research draws on a semi-systematic review of 56 academic case studies, to examine how CBA projects are implemented in practice. The analysis asks which actors are involved, how they contribute to CBA implementation, and which stages of implementation and activities consistently emerge across CBA case studies. Using qualitative thematic analysis, the review maps seven stages of CBA: (i) building partnerships, (ii) mapping context and identifying community concerns, (iii) determining suitable adaptation options, (iv) building capacities, (v) implementing adaptation measures, (vi) monitoring, evaluation, and learning, and (vii) scaling-up and scaling-out. Furthermore, the findings show that actors at local, national, and international levels contribute to CBA implementation, while also revealing the risk of persisting power imbalances that can undermine meaningful participation and long-term sustainability if left unaddressed. Thereby, intermediaries appear as pivotal in bridging knowledge systems and governance levels and addressing power imbalances. Empirical research needs emerge regarding monitoring, evaluation, and learning of CBA, as well as the realisation of scaling in practice.

detail.abstract:
Persistent debates about origins (creation, evolution, cosmology) and operation (causality, probability, relativity) frequently arise from conflicts between observational windows rather than from mutually exclusive truths. Unified Transition Field Theory (UTFT) is proposed as a higher-order transition grammar that reorganizes these explanatory languages as regime-specific descriptions of a single transition field, and fixes an actionable kernel for governance and decision-making.

Public policy, corporate strategy, and financial governance repeatedly fail not primarily because of insufficient resources or poor execution, but because interventions are deployed after systems have already entered transition regimes in which conventional levers lose causal efficacy. This preprint establishes priority for UTFT by fixing its canonical actionable kernel (the Lee Core): Joo-Shik Lee's Path Extinction Principle, Transition Timing Condition, and Stop Rule. Together, these primitives define time as shrinking optionality, specify critical window closure as the boundary of effective intervention, and provide stop-rule governance to prevent resource dissipation and structural lock-in once irreversibility is reached. The paper further outlines the Latent/Emergent Transition Framework (LETF) as an operational detection layer for early transition signals. Domain applications and empirical decision maps are reserved for versioned extensions (v2+).

detail.abstract: This Research Paper addresses the growing problem of access to essential medicines, focusing on the role of intellectual property rights, particularly patent rights, in restricting access by enabling pharmaceutical market monopolies that keep drug prices high. The paper explores the Bolar exception, a legal mechanism designed to allow generic drug manufacturers to seek regulatory approval before a patent expires, thus preventing the de facto extension of patent monopolies. Through this comparative analysis, the paper argues for the broader implementation of Bolar exceptions to improve access to affordable medicines and reduce healthcare costs.

detail.title: Are Households Pareto Efficient? A Test Based on Multiple Job Holding
detail.abstract: The collective household model requires that household decisions result in Pareto efficient outcomes. While this assumption is falsifiable, these tests are often difficult to implement due to data limitations or insufficient statistical power. We identify a novel setting-multiple job holding-where these issues are less of an obstacle. Using data from Bangladesh, we estimate the labor supply of households where members are engaged in multiple occupations and use the parameter estimates to test the collective model. We are unable to reject Pareto efficiency, but do find evidence against the unitary model. The results support the use of the collective model as a framework to study the inner workings of the household.

detail.abstract:
This paper reports and analyzes survey results from 2,792 respondents estimating the probability of a stock market crash (defined as a 30% decline at any point over the next twelve months), collected in connection with our companion paper "How Likely is a Stock Market Crash?" (Haghani and White, 2025).

We document substantial divergence between market-based probability estimates and subjective investor beliefs. Survey respondents reported an average crash probability of 30.5% (median 25%), nearly four times higher than the 8% market-implied probability we derived from equity options prices in our prior paper. Only 31% of respondents estimated probabilities within a factor of two of our market-based estimate. However, among the 820 respondents who revised their estimates after reading our analysis, average probabilities dropped from 34% to 20%, suggesting that many initial estimates reflected limited analysis rather than deeply held convictions.

We contextualize these findings within the behavioral finance literature, particularly Goetzmann, Kim, and Shiller (2024), which attributes elevated subjective crash probabilities to negative emotions and "risk-as-feelings" rather than rational assessment. We challenge respondents who maintain high crash probability estimates with a "put your money where your mouth is" analysis, demonstrating that investors believing in a 30% crash probability should optimally allocate approximately 3% of wealth to out-of-the-money put options (assuming standard risk aversion), creating leveraged downside exposure equal to 3x their wealth. We suspect few respondents would actually implement such a strategy, suggesting a disconnect between stated and revealed preferences.

Drawing on Aumann's Agreement Theorem and incorporating the wisdom of our survey respondents, we update our crash probability estimate from 8% to 11%. We conclude by introducing Brier score methodology for evaluating the historical accuracy of crash predictions and encourage convergence toward more calibrated probability assessments.

detail.abstract: Ceremonial and social expenditures account for a substantial share of household budgets in developing economies and are often justified as investments in social capital and informal insurance. Yet, little is known about how households protect essential consumption—particularly food—when ceremonial obligations increase, and the role credit plays in this process. Using household panel data, this study examines how ceremonial spending interacts with different forms of credit to shape food consumption. We conceptualize credit as operating through two channels: a protective role that relaxes liquidity constraints and enables consumption smoothing, and a pressurizing role embedded in social financial institutions that intensifies repayment and social obligations. Employing household fixed-effects models, we show that ceremonial spending is positively associated with food expenditure on average. This association is significantly stronger for households with access to credit and for those borrowing specifically for medical and household consumption purposes. In contrast, participation in credit and savings groups weakens this relationship, indicating a credit pressure channel. The findings are robust to alternative loan definitions and sample restrictions and highlight the importance of distinguishing between protective and pressurizing forms of credit in policy design.

detail.abstract: Illness and disease know no geographic or jurisdictional borders. As such, health care worker migration is an essential component of health care delivery. The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union outlines parameters for the free movement of workers. Rights to such free movement extend to physicians and health care workers. Foreign physicians in the European Union encounter a host of legal, professional, and social barriers to their integration and incorporation as fully certified members of the health care work force in their respective European Union nations. These barriers include language, variations in licensing requirements, patient safety, quality of care, variations in treatment experience, cultural differences, and discrimination. This chapter will examine the legal concerns which prohibit many foreign health care professionals from being extended full health care practice privileges, along with creative ways European Union countries are working to break down barriers to immigrant health care work force entry.

detail.abstract: In a global context marked by accelerating climate change, demographic pressures, and recurring economic challenges, building the resilience of farmers and rural entrepreneurs, alongside ensuring the sustainability of food systems, has become a critical priority for regional development. Mountain areas, often marginalized by conventional financing policies, require tailored financial mechanisms to enhance economic adaptability, foster rural entrepreneurship, and secure food systems. This paper aims to investigate the role of innovative financial instruments, including microfinance, indexed agricultural insurance, and payment schemes for ecosystem services, in supporting the mountain economy, strengthening rural entrepreneurial initiatives, and promoting sustainable local food chains. The study employs a mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative analysis of policy frameworks and existing funding programs in mountain regions of Romania and other European countries with quantitative evaluation of these instruments' impact on economic performance, farmers' adaptability, and rural entrepreneurship development. The research includes case studies from agriculturally and agro-touristically active mountain areas, correlated with statistical data on access to finance, levels of economic diversification, and the capacity to respond to climatic or market shocks. Findings demonstrate that implementing financial instruments adapted to the unique characteristics of mountain regions significantly enhances economic resilience and the sustainability of agri-food systems. The most effective initiatives combine financial support with entrepreneurial education, vocational training, and incentives for agroecological practices. Additionally, the presence of local financial intermediaries, such as cooperatives and local action groups, facilitates the dissemination of these solutions and encourages the growth of rural entrepreneurship in mountain communities. This paper introduces a novel conceptual framework for financing resilience in the mountain economy, moving beyond isolated support measures to focus on regenerative and inclusive financial systems. Contrary to classical approaches, the research integrates territorial, entrepreneurial, social, and ecological dimensions of finance, providing practical insights for policy formulation adapted to mountain regions. The empirical findings highlight the scalability potential of innovative financial solutions that balance rural entrepreneurship development, agricultural productivity, environmental protection, and social cohesion.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how credit supply shocks impact firm-level investment across the euro area using the novel AnaCredit database. detail.title: Adaptive Fraud Detection in Blockchain Payment Systems Using Deep Learning
detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of blockchain-based payment systems has revolutionized financial transactions by offering decentralized, secure, and transparent mechanisms. However, the anonymity and immutability of blockchain also present significant opportunities for fraudulent activities, making fraud detection a critical concern. Traditional rule-based and statistical methods for fraud detection often struggle to cope with the evolving and sophisticated nature of blockchain fraud, necessitating more adaptive and intelligent solutions. This study proposes an adaptive fraud detection framework for blockchain payment systems utilizing deep learning techniques. The framework leverages historical transaction data, behavioral patterns, and network features to identify anomalous activities indicative of potential fraud. Advanced deep learning models, including recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and graph neural networks (GNNs), are employed to capture temporal dependencies and relational patterns in transaction networks. The model is designed to continuously learn from new data, improving its detection accuracy over time and adapting to emerging fraudulent strategies. Experimental evaluation on real-world blockchain transaction datasets demonstrates that the proposed system achieves high precision, recall, and F1-score, outperforming conventional machine learning and rule-based methods. The findings indicate that deep learning-based adaptive detection can significantly enhance the security and reliability of blockchain payment systems. This research contributes to the fields of financial cybersecurity, blockchain analytics, and intelligent fraud prevention, offering practical solutions for safeguarding decentralized financial ecosystems.

detail.abstract:
This book analyzes the key features of the fiscal system and the various factors underlying the development of tax systems. In examining fiscal policy, particular attention is given to the effects and consequences of different tax types and rates, with a specific focus on Value Added Tax (VAT). Well-designed fiscal policies can facilitate faster economic development, depending on each country’s economic conditions and fiscal capacity, with particular reference to the Republic of Kosovo.

A comparison of tax systems across countries reveals that no two systems are implemented in exactly the same manner. This variation arises from the interaction of diverse economic, institutional, and social factors. In Kosovo, tax revenues represent the primary source of budget financing, with VAT playing a central role.

Accordingly, Kosovo’s tax system has evolved over time through gradual alignment with European Union regulations, while preserving national specificities. Value Added Tax is applied in all European Union member states, as well as in several countries in Asia and Latin America. Nevertheless, VAT is most closely associated with the European Union, where it is mandatory and largely harmonized under the Sixth VAT Directive.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a minimal dynamic model of automation and artificial intelligence that emphasizes task-level substitution and ownership of automation rents. Production combines routine and non-routine tasks, with automation capital substituting for labor only within the routine domain. In a two-period overlapping generations economy with automation-capital accumulation and heterogeneous ownership, I show that when task-level substitutability is high and ownership of automation capital is sufficiently concentrated, a wage-only income system cannot sustain a stationary equilibrium with full absorption of output. In this regime, profits rise and wage income falls while the marginal product of automation capital saturates, generating structural excess saving relative to investment. Transfers funded by automation rents (profit sharing or social dividends) emerge as equilibrium-restoring rather than redistributive, and labor supply becomes a secondary adjustment margin. The results are conditional and non-deterministic: when substitution is limited, ownership is broad, or task creation offsets automation, the wage-based regime remains viable.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a fixed-point instrumental variables (FP-IV) estimator for linear feedback systems in which all regressors are endogenous and no external instruments are available. The approach exploits residuals generated within the system itself and defines the estimator as the fixed point of a residual-based instrumental variables mapping. A central insight of the paper is that identification emerges at convergence.At the fixed point, residual-based instruments coincide with the underlying structural shocks and satisfy the orthogonality conditions required for instrumental variables estimation. Under a mild stability condition ensuring contraction of the population mapping, the fixed point exists and is unique, and the resulting estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the theoretical results. The FP-IV estimator converges reliably, exhibits negligible bias, and delivers well-calibrated inference across a range of designs. The numerical evidence also highlights a structural implication of the approach: at least three nodes are required for identification, while two-node feedback systems typically fail to converge. The results demonstrate that credible causal inference in feedback systems does not require external instruments when the economic structure generates sufficiently rich multi-node interactions.

title: Success, Social Power, and the Forgotten Vote of Consumers

detail.title: Success, Social Power, and the Forgotten Vote of Consumers
detail.abstract: Success is often treated as a personal achievement and wealth as a sign of a better life. This paper argues that such views misunderstand both success and wealth. First, success is not a transformation of human life itself, but an expansion of social power. Second, wealth does not alter the fundamental structure of human existence, but reorganizes control over resources and people. Third, the social power of successful individuals is not inherent; it is collectively granted by society, especially by consumers, through everyday actions. Finally, this paper argues that if this collective " granting " is understood as a form of voting, it can be consciously redirected to build a more equal and humane society. Recognizing consumer behavior as a political and ethical act is essential for reclaiming public power and reshaping social outcomes..

detail.abstract: Leadership is enacted not only through formal authority and decisions but also through the stories leaders tell about organizational futures. In small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), where leaders and employees work in close proximity, such vision narratives are closely scrutinized and may play a crucial role in shaping employees’ experiences at work. This research proposal examines how leaders’ vision narratives, as perceived by employees in terms of authenticity and coherence, influence employee well-being and, in turn, their willingness to engage in championing behavior—defined as the persistent advocacy and implementation of new ideas despite obstacles. Drawing on sensemaking theory, conservation of resources theory, and social identity perspectives, the study conceptualizes leaders’ vision narratives as potential psychological and identity-based resources that help employees cope with uncertainty and sustain proactive behavior. The research adopts a sequential mixed-methods design. An initial qualitative phase explores how employees interpret and evaluate leaders’ vision stories in everyday organizational settings, followed by a quantitative phase testing the proposed relationships across SMEs in Pakistan’s renewable-energy sector. The study aims to contribute to leadership and innovation research by highlighting the role of narrative quality in fostering well-being and innovation-related behaviors in resource-constrained organizational contexts.

title: Automated Validation Frameworks for Federal Reserve CCAR Stress Testing: Architecture, Implementation, and Production Results from 15+ Regulatory Cycles

detail.title: Automated Validation Frameworks for Federal Reserve CCAR Stress Testing: Architecture, Implementation, and Production Results from 15+ Regulatory Cycles
detail.abstract: The Federal Reserve's Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) represents the most stringent stress testing regime for large U.S. financial institutions, requiring submission of highly complex capital projections under severely adverse economic scenarios with zero tolerance for material errors. This paper presents an automated validation framework deployed across 15+ consecutive CCAR cycles at a major financial institution, processing 50,000+ validation rules across capital, risk-weighted assets, and pre-provision net revenue calculations. Our framework addresses four critical challenges: (1) automated validation of complex regulatory calculations spanning hundreds of interconnected models; (2) detection and prevention of data quality issues, calculation errors, and regulatory interpretation gaps; (3) workflow orchestration supporting iterative model refinement under compressed timelines; and (4) comprehensive audit trail generation for regulatory examination and internal governance. Deployed continuously over five years including operation through evolving regulatory requirements and institutional changes, the framework achieved 40% reduction in validation cycle time (10 days to 6 days), 60% reduction in submission defects detected by Federal Reserve review, 75% reduction in postsubmission adjustments, and zero material qualification findings across all cycles. We present architectural decisions, validation pattern libraries, regulatory interpretation approaches, operational lessons learned, and recommendations for practitioners implementing automated validation in highly regulated environments. Our contributions provide concrete guidance for deploying production-grade regulatory validation while advancing understanding of quality assurance in complex compliance contexts.

detail.abstract: Economic analysis relies fundamentally on measurement, yet the nature of economic measurement is often conflated with estimation, statistical testing, or prediction in empirical research. This paper develops a conceptual framework that clarifies what economics measures and how it operates at different analytical levels. It distinguishes among the measurement of economic data, marginal economic relationships, and systemwide economic structures and equilibrium states. Within this framework, standard econometrics is shown to be well suited for measuring marginal relationships under uncertainty, but limited in its ability to assess structural consistency and endogenous adjustment when accounting identities impose closure. Drawing on the dual legacy of least squares associated with Legendre and Gauss, the paper highlights alternative interpretations of deviations and residuals as adjustment mechanisms rather than purely stochastic noise. The paper provides a theoretical foundation for interpreting empirical models more precisely and for aligning econometric hypotheses with economic meaning.

detail.abstract: Repeated false alarms for adverse weather events can undermine public trust, potentially leading to a reluctance in taking appropriate actions, such as evacuation. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms by which false alarms influence perceptions and actions is essential for building socially effective early warning systems (EWS). We aimed to examine perceptions, emotions, and actions regarding false flood warnings in Japan. Specifically, we investigated (1) people’s definition of hits; (2) emotional responses toward false alarms; (3) the effect of the false alarm ratio (FAR) on the perceived FAR (pFAR) and the heterogeneity of this effect according to participants’ definition of hits; and (4) the effect of pFAR on evacuation action and the heterogeneity of this effect according to the emotional responses toward false alarms. We used municipality-level FAR data newly derived for this study and questionnaire data collected from residents of the Kyushu Region (n = 997). The results showed that participants tended to consider a warning as a hit when the river water reached a hazardous water level or when an overflow or levee breach occurred. Furthermore, when a false alarm occurred, negative emotions such as sadness and anger tended to decrease, whereas positive emotions such as being pleased and at ease tended to increase. We found a non-significant relationship between FAR and pFAR, which was maintained regardless of the participants’ hit definitions. However, we found that pFAR had a significantly negative effect on the probability of evacuation, and this negative effect was weaker among those who experienced positive emotions toward false alarms. These findings suggest that effective EWS require not only improvements in scientific warning accuracy but also risk communication strategies that consider emotional responses to false alarms.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive review and analysis of New China's economic development strategy from 1949 to 1978. Drawing on a wide range of literature, by Chinese scholars and the key contributions from western researchers ， the study examines the evolution of national economic policy through three phases: the Industrialization Phase, the "Surpass Britain and Catch the US" stage, and the preliminary stage of the Four Modernization. Through a detailed literature review, analysis of adjustment stages, evaluation of the major achievements, and the quantitative assessments, this paper elucidates the underlying reasons behind strategic adjustments, the statistical outcomes of various policies, and the long-term impact of these early strategies on China's post-1978 reform trajectory. title: The Excluded Worker: Tracing the Structural Limits of India’s Labour Law in a Capitalist Economy

detail.title: The Excluded Worker: Tracing the Structural Limits of India’s Labour Law in a Capitalist Economy
detail.abstract: India’s labour law framework systematically excludes 82-90% of the workforce through coordinated legal mechanisms that prioritise capital flexibility over worker protection. This research demonstrates that exclusion is not a regulatory gap, but rather an intentional design embedded in the CoSS 2020. Through doctrinal analysis of constitutional jurisprudence, empirical examination of published judicial data, and comparative legal analysis of peer emerging economies, this study establishes five novel propositions: Constitutional Piercing Doctrine permits courts to disregard contractual classifications when they defeat fundamental rights; Algorithmic opacity violates Article 23’s forced labour prohibition; Multi-platform work intensifies subordination contrary to “independence” fictions; Published judicial delay data concentrates disadvantage on vulnerable workers; and CoSS 2020 represents deliberate policy choice favouring welfare-exclusion over employment rights. The research contributes a prescriptive framework for Algorithmic Due Process (ADP) as a mandatory constitutional standard, establishing that Indian labour law functions as a successful technology for institutionalising precarious labour within capitalist accumulation.

detail.abstract: This paper aims to provide a constitutional-level solution to the unrestrained expansion of the modern state's fiscal power-what Buchanan described as "Leviathan." We argue that traditional democratic procedures (such as elections) have proven insufficient to effectively constrain the state's taxing and spending behavior, leading to persistent fiscal deficits and government failure. The core argument of this paper is that the root of the problem is not policy error, but a flaw in the fiscal constitution itself: the state's monopoly on the right of disposition over tax revenues. To rectify this flaw, we construct a new fiscal constitution called the "Citizen's Executive Right" (CER). Through institutional arrangements such as a dual-track tax system, Personal Public Accounts (PPAs), and competitive Public Governance Organizations (PGOs), this constitution returns the right of disposition over the majority of tax revenues from the state's agent (the government) to the sovereign (the citizens). We further argue that a macro-signal endogenously emerging from this mechanism-the "Total Lapsing Rate" (Λt)-functionally plays the role of a procedural, non-personified "Wicksellian rule of unanimity," ensuring that public expenditures are value-enhancing. The conclusion of this paper is that the CER framework provides a logically self-consistent and operational constitutional option for constraining the fiscal Leviathan, solving the Hayekian "knowledge problem," and achieving a voluntarily cooperative "Creative Commonwealth.

English Abstract: This paper explores the copyright implications of training generative AI models on protected images, questioning whether such use constitutes infringement or falls under the "Fair Use" doctrine. While current legal frameworks in Israel and the US - reliant on the "transformative use" test (as seen in Google Books) - might technically permit such training, the paper argues this creates an "inverse market failure." Unlike previous technologies (e.g., in the Sony case) that opened new markets without eliminating the old, generative AI threatens to replace human creators entirely, thereby nullifying the incentive to create.

To resolve the tension between fostering technological innovation and preserving human creativity, the author proposes a "Differential Regulation" model. This approach distinguishes between artistic contributions based on their cultural value: granting robust protection to "high-contribution" works to maintain creative incentives, while classifying the use of generic or "low-contribution" works as fair use to fuel AI development. The paper suggests a hybrid mechanism allowing artists to opt for compensation or exclusion, offering a nuanced legal solution that sustains both the AI industry and the artistic community.
